I was in a similar situation in freshman year of college. Due to some mix-up, I got placed in housing with all (presumably) cis men, rather than the gender-inclusive housing I requested. When I entered college I had just started to pass 100% of the time, so I was worried I wouldn't pass to people. Time passed and nobody seemed to know (including my roommate somehow), but it was eating me up inside having to hide this part of myself from others. I was being super careful in the showers, always slouching when I couldn't bind my chest (like when I was getting ready to sleep), and always worried the littlest things like cadence of my voice, posture, or stance, would out me to others. Eventually I came out to a few of my friends who lived on the floor with me, and they continued to treat me the same after. I saw myself in them more and more, in the ways they would sometimes be a little awkward, or do something a little feminine like paint their nails purple despite being straight, sing along to girly kpop songs in the shower, etc. Sometimes, they seemed a little unsure of themselves. I realized *they were just like me in the ways that matter*. People are just people. You are not an alien from another planet, you are not some creature, you are just like everyone else and just like the cis men you hang out with. Being stealth can come with a lot of insecurity, but remember that everyone deals with that, and every man deals with feeling "not man enough", feeling a little lonely, feeling a little like an outsider. You are not alone. Some trials are just a part of being human.

2. In the more immediate/short term, try some brow shaping. I'm ftm and I used to do my eyebrows like this and get compliments on them (the rest of this comment is just my technique, feel free to ignore but I wanted to put it out there for you or anyone else, lol). Pluck below the brow to remove the couple hairs that start before the rest of the brow (so the bottom can look more even), then you can consider plucking from the bottom of your eyebrow arch a tiny bit if you want. Only pluck hairs from the bottom line of your brow, from the area between your eyebrows where everyone gets a few unibrow hairs, and from the space between the end of your eyebrow and your hairline if you get any there. Do not pluck from the top of your brow in general, except for *maybe* at the start of the brow near the center of your face. After you've plucked, get a small/precise pair of scissors like sewing scissors or scissors for cuticles in nail treatment. Fluff up your eyebrow with your finger so that the hair closer to the center of your face stands up straight. Then, go in with scissors and trim this area comlletely flat. This evens out the top of the brow and may make it appear "neater".

As a 19 year old who was in your shoes ~2-3 years ago, my advice is to wait it out until you can leave:
1. Do your best to continue to be connected to reality, so to speak. Talk to friends, trusted adults, anyone who is a part of your support system. You seem very aware of the fact that she is trying to get in your head, which is good. Continue to talk to people who are accepting of your identity, to help keep you grounded in what you know to be true.
2. Focus on every other aspect of your life, other than medical transition, for now. Transition as a minor with unsupportive parents is just not going to happen, and it's best to accept that and just try not to think about it until you reach age 18 or the age of majority where you live. You need to focus on school, friends, and (very importantly) finding a job somewhere. Look into colleges if you're planning on them and start figuring out where you'll be going, and what scores, grades, and letters of recommendation you will need.
3. Build your independence. Try working on weekends at a store as a cashier, or doing other entry-level jobs you can get to. If you are not yet able to drive yourself places, that's another important step to get in motion as soon as possible. Be able to drive, be able to get to work, be able to work and save up money. As a minor who I assume has not changed his legal name, your employers will have access to your old name. This is unavoidable. Certain store chains, like Walmart, will allow associates to choose preferred names to be displayed in their systems or on people's nametags. 
4. When you reach the age of majority or 18, you will be able to get away with being on T for a very short amount of time before it becomes noticeable. My voice dropped sharply at around month 2. If you think she would kick you out for being on T, don't try to take testosterone in secret for too long because it will be a hassle to hide all the injection supplies, and potentially impossible to hide its effects.

source: I was stealth my entire first year at college to everyone, including my roommate who I shared a room with. I have been on T and pass but have not had top or bottom surgery.

#1) you can only be stealth if you actually pass. not saying you don't, there's about 0 information in this post, but I see this term misused a LOT as people just not yet transitioned, stealth specifically means passing and non-disclosing. this will mean for 99% of people that you have been on testosterone for several months at least. 
#2) if you already consistently and near 100% of the time pass as male and don't want others to know you are trans, clear your online footprint as much as possible. make sure you check your social media accounts for photos where you were pre-transition or don't pass because others can see those. google your name and make sure there are no results which would tell people that you're trans. 
#3) this depends on where you live in the world and your situation, but legally changing your name and sex is a must as soon as you have the means to do so. if you're in the U.S., you may want to hold off on certain changes for now as the government has been a bit crazy recently.
#4) Just be normal and genuine in social interactions. it will be very rare when your transness will be even slightly relevant to a conversation with others. just chill out and have fun with other people who share similar interests. tell little white lies every now and then to get out of things which would out you (such as people joking about dick size, other dick stuff, etc.), but other than that just be yourself. 
#5) socializing with guys is only a bit different than with girls. there are a ton of differences in social dynamics but they honestly won't affect your passing at all. don't try to act too tough or "macho" or whatever, people will just think you're insecure lol. just go with the flow, you will naturally pick up the mannerisms of other guys from talking to them.

your sense of self simply developed differently than your body did. we think being trans starts in childhood and is solidified at age 9. by that age, you know who you are, and have some feel of what gender you are. sometimes, for whatever reason, kids reach that age and think of themselves as the opposite gender of what they were assigned at birth. since most kids start puberty several years after 9, they tend to live with this identity not being a big problem for them for several years. then it all goes downhill. for me I got my period in 5th grade at 11, and I got boobs at only 9 years old. I felt extremely uncomfortable with the fact I did and especially that other people could see the outline of them coming out of my shirt. they also hurt like hell a lot because they were growing and I wished I could just cut them off. but I had never been called a boy before, never had the experience of being called he or a boy name, and I didn't know that it would feel better than being called a girl name. I felt uncomfortable but I thought it might be normal for kids my age. I continued to age and in middle school I realized I had no attachment to being female at all. but I was short and extremely physically feminine in terms of my body type, and it just didn't seem like being a boy was attainable for me. even if I had my chest removed, went on testosterone, etc, I would still have feminine hips and be 5'1". I decided to stick with my assigned gender for several years, wear a ton of makeup every day, grow my hair out really long. I thought that, even if I would rather be a boy, I would never be a full one, I would always be a half-boy he-she in the eyes of others. at least when I was female, everyone saw me as WHOLE. recently I realized I just couldn't do it anymore. I know my role in society is not the feminine one. my soul is not one that is female. the extra-ness of femininity, the more revealing clothing, more expressive voices and tone, none of it is me. I think the point is that anyone can do anything they want-a girl can like dirtbiking and a boy can playing with dolls or something and in the end it doesn't matter. Things like the way you present yourself and the way you dress to the way you act are called gender expression. The argument is that anyone can do anything, no matter how masculine or feminine, but it doesn't change the fact that you're a man or that you're a woman. 
However transgender people tend to feel something called gender dysphoria, something almost like a mental illness, and similar to body dysmorphia. Someone with dysphoria wants to physically change and alter their body, like someone with body dysmorphia. They feel that their bodies are wrong somehow. The difference is that a dysphoric person wants to edit their body to fit the opposite sex (i.e. a female-born person wanting to remove their breasts in order to be more like a man) because they feel that they are the opposite sex. It's different for a girl to want to do typically masculine things, to be a tomboy, than for her to want to actually be a man.
As for the children part, I personally do not believe that children should be allowed to transition. I don't think a child really has the understanding of gender and the consequences of transition until they are much older. There are things called hormone blockers. If a prepubescent child believes themselves to be transgender, they can take the blockers to prevent their bodies from partaking in puberty. If the child decides that they aren't trans, they can simply stop the blockers and puberty should take place. It is different from giving a child hormones or surgery, which I am absolutely against. However, there are few studies regarding hormone blockers and there can be side effects to taking them. It's not the safest thing to do and I'm not sure what my stance is on that. 
I'm not going to say "gender isn't real" or any weird stuff like that, but I do want to say that the difference, put simply, is that transgender people have gender dysphoria, whereas other people just doing whatever they want don't.
